emeritus

ih-MER-ih-tus -- usually follows a professional title, as in 'professor emeritus.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Emeritus is retired from a position but retaining the title as an honor.

After forty years teaching chemistry, she retired with the title of professor emeritus.

Example

A longtime CEO steps down from running the company day-to-day but is still invited to board meetings and listed on the letterhead as chairman emeritus.

That honorary continuation of a title after retirement is exactly what emeritus describes. Unlike 'former,' which simply means no longer holding a role, emeritus specifically signals an honor bestowed at retirement.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

honorary: Honorary describes a title granted purely as a mark of respect rather than earned by actually holding the job -- an honorary degree, for example. Emeritus is different: the person truly served in the position for years and keeps its title only after retiring from it.

former: Former simply means no longer holding a role -- a former mayor, a former coach. It marks only that the time in the job has ended. Emeritus goes further: the person keeps the title after retiring, carried as an honor for long service.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

active: currently working in a role or position

incoming: about to begin a role or position

Where it sits · how much honor comes with it — retired → emeritus → distinguished

retired vs. emeritus: Retired is more general than emeritus -- retired simply means no longer working, while emeritus specifically signals that a retiring person keeps their title as a mark of honor.

distinguished vs. emeritus: Distinguished can feel like an even higher level of honor than emeritus: emeritus specifically marks the transition into retirement, while distinguished can describe ongoing, active excellence throughout an entire career.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — e-

Prefix — e-: out, thoroughly (a form of Latin ex-)

Root — merit

Root — merit: to earn, deserve (from Latin merere -- the same root as merit)

Suffix — -us

Suffix — -us: the Latin adjective ending, kept when English borrowed the word whole

Put it together

Put it together: E- ('out, thoroughly') + merit ('to earn, deserve', from Latin merere) + -us (the Latin ending the word kept) spell emeritus. Latin emeritus meant 'having served one's time, having thoroughly earned it' -- someone titled emeritus has fully earned the honor of keeping their title after stepping down, the same root that gives us merit.

Use the root in a new word: merit

Use the root in a new word: merit: The scholarship was awarded purely on merit, based on years of outstanding grades.

Emeritus almost always follows the noun it describes, as in 'professor emeritus' or 'CEO emeritus,' and is used only after someone has retired from that role.
